questions.question: Which one of the following kinds of derivation is used by LR parsers?
questions.explanation:
An LR parser works bottom-up: it repeatedly reduces handles. The sequence of reductions is exactly a rightmost derivation traced in reverse.

Answer: Rightmost in reverse

questions.question: Which ONE of the following statements is FALSE regarding the symbol table?

options.A: Symbol table is responsible for keeping track of the scope of variables.
options.B: Symbol table can be implemented using a binary search tree.
options.C: Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase.
options.D: Symbol table is created during the lexical analysis phase.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement about the symbol table:

- It tracks variable scope — true, this is one of its core jobs.
- It can be implemented using a BST — true, BSTs (or hash tables) are standard implementations.
- It is created during lexical analysis — true, entries are typically first added as identifiers are tokenized.
- "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase" — FALSE. The symbol table is essential well beyond parsing: semantic analysis (type checking), intermediate code generation, and code optimization (e.g. register allocation) all continue to rely on it.

Answer: "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase" is FALSE.

questions.question:
Consider the following C statements:

char *str1 = "Hello; /* Statement S1 */
char *str2 = "Hello;"; /* Statement S2 */
int *str3 = "Hello"; /* Statement S3 */

Which of the following options is/are correct?

options.B: [latex]\text{S2}[/latex] has a lexical error and [latex]\text{S3}[/latex] has a syntactic error
options.C: [latex]\text{S1}[/latex] has a lexical error and [latex]\text{S3}[/latex] has a semantic error
options.D: [latex]\text{S1}[/latex] has a syntactic error and [latex]\text{S3}[/latex] has a semantic error

questions.explanation:
[latex]\text{S1: char *str1 = "Hello;}[/latex] — the string literal is missing its closing double-quote. An unterminated string literal is a lexical error (the lexer/scanner cannot even form a valid string token).

[latex]\text{S2: char *str2 = "Hello;";}[/latex] — this is a perfectly valid string literal (containing a semicolon character) assigned to a [latex]\text{char *}[/latex]; no error at all.

[latex]\text{S3: int *str3 = "Hello";}[/latex] — this is lexically and syntactically fine (a valid string literal, valid statement syntax), but it assigns a [latex]\text{char *}[/latex] value to an incompatible [latex]\text{int *}[/latex] pointer type. This is a type-mismatch, which is a semantic error (caught during semantic/type analysis, not parsing).

Answer: S1 has a lexical error, and S3 has a semantic error.

questions.question:
Consider the following grammar along with translation rules.
[latex] \begin{aligned} &S \rightarrow S_1 \# T & & \{S._{val}=S_{1.val}*T._{val} \} \\ &S \rightarrow T & & \{S._{val}=T._{val} \} \\ &T \rightarrow T_1 \% R & & \{T._{val}=T_{1.val} \div R._{val} \} \\ &T \rightarrow R & & \{T._{val}=R._{val} \} \\ &R \rightarrow id & & \{R._{val}=id._{val} \} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Here [latex] \#[/latex] and [latex] \%[/latex] are operators and [latex]id[/latex] is a token that represents an integer and [latex]id_{.val}[/latex] represents the corresponding integer value. The set of non-terminals is [latex] \{S,T,R,P \}[/latex] and a subscripted non-terminal indicates an instance of the non-terminal.
Using this translation scheme, the computed value of [latex]S_{.val}[/latex] for root of the parse tree for the expression [latex]20 \# 10 \% 5 \# 8 \% 2 \% 2[/latex] is
questions.explanation:
From the grammar, # (multiply) is at the S level, so it has lower precedence; % (divide) is at the T level, so it binds tighter. Both are left recursive, i.e. left associative.

[latex]20\,\#\,(10\%5)\,\#\,((8\%2)\%2)=20\times2\times2=80[/latex]

Answer: 80

questions.question:
The program below uses six temporary variables a, b, c, d, e, f.

a =1
b= 10
c =20
d= a +b
e= c +d
f =c +e
b= c+ e
e =b +f
d =5 +e
return d +f

Assuming that all operations take their operands from registers, what is the minimum number of registers needed to execute this program without spilling?

At most 3 values are live at once.

questions.question:
Refer to the given 3-address code sequence. This code sequence is split into basic blocks. The number of basic blocks is _________. (Answer in integer)

1001: i = 1
1002: j = 1
1003: t1 = 10*i
1004: t2 = t1+j
1005: t3 = 8*t2
1006: t4 = t3-88
1007: a[t4] = 0.0
1008: j = j+1
1009: if j <= 10 goto 1003
1010: i = i+1
1011: if i <= 10 goto 1002
1012: i = 1
1013: t5 = i-1
1014: t6 = 88*t5
1015: a[t6] = 1.0
1016: i = i+1
1017: if i <= 10 goto 1013
questions.explanation:
A new basic block begins at every leader statement: the very first statement, any statement that is the target of a jump/goto, and any statement immediately following a conditional or unconditional jump.

Scanning the code for leaders: [latex]1001[/latex] (first statement); [latex]1003[/latex] (target of the [latex]\text{goto }1003[/latex] at [latex]1009[/latex]); [latex]1010[/latex] (follows the conditional jump at [latex]1009[/latex]); [latex]1002[/latex] (target of [latex]\text{goto }1002[/latex] at [latex]1011[/latex]); [latex]1012[/latex] (follows the conditional jump at [latex]1011[/latex]); [latex]1013[/latex] (target of [latex]\text{goto }1013[/latex] at [latex]1017[/latex]).

That's [latex]6[/latex] leaders, giving [latex]6[/latex] basic blocks: [latex]\{1001\},\{1002\},\{1003\text{-}1009\},\{1010\text{-}1011\},\{1012\},\{1013\text{-}1017\}[/latex].

Answer: 6

questions.question:
C onsider the following parse tree for the expression a#b$c$d#e#f, involving two binary operators $ and #.

Which one of the following is correct for the given parse tree?

options.A: [latex]\$[/latex] has higher precedence and is left associative; # is right associative
options.B: # has higher precedence and is left associative; [latex]\$[/latex] is right associative
options.C: [latex]\$[/latex] has higher precedence and is left associative; # is left associative
options.D: # has higher precedence and is right associative; [latex]\$[/latex] is left associative

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- $ appears deeper in the tree than #, so it is applied first [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] $ has higher precedence.
- b $ c $ d is grouped as (b $ c) $ d [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] $ is left associative.
- a # ([latex]\ldots[/latex] # (e # f)) groups to the right [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] # is right associative.

Answer: $ has higher precedence and is left associative; # is right associative

questions.question: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE while computing [latex]First[/latex] and [latex]Follow[/latex] during top-down parsing by a compiler?

options.A: For a production [latex]A \to \epsilon ,  \epsilon [/latex] will be added to [latex]First(A) [/latex].
options.B: If there is any input right end marker, it will be added to[latex] First(S) [/latex], where [latex] S [/latex] is the start symbol.
options.C: For a production [latex] A \to \epsilon,  \epsilon [/latex] will be added to [latex] Follow(A) [/latex].
options.D: If there is any input right end marker, it will be added to [latex] Follow(S) [/latex], where [latex] S [/latex] is the start symbol.

questions.explanation:
Standard rules for computing [latex]\text{First}[/latex] and [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] sets:

- "For [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex], add [latex]\epsilon[/latex] to First(A)": TRUE — this is exactly the base rule for handling nullable productions in First-set computation.
- "If there's an input right-end marker, add it to First(S)": FALSE — the end marker [latex]\$[/latex] belongs in [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] sets (marking "nothing more can follow"), never in a [latex]\text{First}[/latex] set.
- "For [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex], add [latex]\epsilon[/latex] to Follow(A)": FALSE — [latex]\epsilon[/latex] is never placed into any [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] set; [latex]\text{Follow}[/latex] sets only ever contain actual terminals (and possibly [latex]\$[/latex]).
- "If there's an input right-end marker, add it to Follow(S)": TRUE — this is the standard initialization rule, since nothing legitimately follows the start symbol except the end of input.

Answer: "ε is added to First(A) for A→ε" and "the end marker is added to Follow(S)" are both TRUE.

questions.question:
Consider the control flow graph given below.

Which one of the following options is the set of live variables at the exit point of each basic block?
questions.explanation:
This is a standard backward liveness-analysis question based on the accompanying control-flow graph. Liveness is computed backward through the CFG using [latex]\text{live-in}(B)=\text{use}(B)\cup\big(\text{live-out}(B)-\text{def}(B)\big)[/latex] and [latex]\text{live-out}(B)=\bigcup_{\text{succ }S}\text{live-in}(S)[/latex], iterating until the sets stabilize.

Working from the exit block backward (where no variables are live at the very end), and propagating each block's used-but-not-yet-redefined variables up to its predecessors, the live-out sets that satisfy this fixpoint for the given graph are: [latex]B1:\{a,b,c,e,f\}[/latex], [latex]B2:\{d,e\}[/latex], [latex]B3:\{b,c,e,f\}[/latex], and [latex]B4:\phi[/latex] (empty, since it's the exit).

Answer: B1:{a,b,c,e,f}, B2:{d,e}, B3:{b,c,e,f}, B4:φ

questions.question:
A variable x is said to be live at a statement [latex]S_{i}[/latex] in a program if the following three conditions hold simultaneously:
i. There exists a statement [latex]S_{j}[/latex] that uses x
ii. There is a path from [latex]S_{i}[/latex] to [latex]S_{j}[/latex] in the flow graph corresponding to the program
iii. The path has no intervening assignment to x including at [latex]S_{i}[/latex] and [latex]S_{j}[/latex]

The variables which are live both at the statement in basic block 2 and at the statement in basic block 3 of the above control flow graph are
questions.explanation:
Live-in = use [latex]\cup[/latex] (live-out [latex]-[/latex] def).

- Block 1 uses q, r, v before defining them [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] in(1) = {q, r, v}
- in(4) = {v, r} [latex]\cup[/latex] (in(1) [latex]-[/latex] {q}) = {r, v}
- in(2) = {r, u} [latex]\cup[/latex] (in(4) [latex]-[/latex] {v}) = {r, u}
- in(3) = {s, u} [latex]\cup[/latex] (in(4) [latex]-[/latex] {q}) = {r, s, u, v}

Common: r, u

Answer: r, u
